extracted.intended_audience: aspiring satirists/poets and literate readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for composing satire in verse: what to aim at, how to choose targets, tonal limits, rhetorical methods (example vs. precept), and language register for serious topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim satire at falsehood, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: “The aim of the true satirist is not to be severe upon persons, but only upon falsehood.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select individuals only insofar as they personify the bad principle to be exposed; use particular lives and characters to make abstract bad principles comprehensible. The satirist's purpose is to follow falsehood after it diverges and show it 'floundering in the bog at the end of it.' Avoid gratuitous personal cruelty—attack the error, not the human being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer example over abstruse precept
rubrics_metrics.description: “A bad principle is comparatively harmless while it continues to be an abstraction, nor can the general mind comprehend it fully till it is printed in that large type which all men can read at sight, namely, the life and character, the sayings and doings, of particular persons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples, characters, and illustrative scenes rather than long didactic exposition; show the consequences of the error through narrative or caricature to make satire effective ('Longum iter per præcepta, breve et efficace per exempla').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise restraint — avoid excessive harshness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The danger of the satirist is, that continual use may deaden his sensibility to the force of language. He becomes more and more liable to strike harder than he knows or intends.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor tone and severity; be careful not to 'strike harder than he knows or intends.' Use measured devices (metaphor: put on boxing-gloves) and remember that increased practice can blunt judgment and lead to cruelty or excess. Prefer tasteful, controlled ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper ridicule with good-nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a kind of weapon that must have a button of good-nature on the point of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when sharp, satire should carry a core of good temper or benevolence so it reads as corrective rather than vindictive. The 'button of good-nature' moderates the sting and preserves the satirist's moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to ridicule Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Truth is quite beyond the reach of satire. There is so brave a simplicity in her, that she can no more be made ridiculous than an oak or a pine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of satire: aim at hypocrisy, error, and falsehood. Truth's inherent dignity cannot be plausibly mocked; misdirecting satire at truly virtuous positions is both ineffective and improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gentle wit (Attic salt) over corrosive vitriol (aqua fortis)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He were a sorry gardener who should wage a whole day's war with an iron scuffle on those ill weeds that make the garden-walks of life unsightly, when a sprinkle of Attic salt will wither them up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use light, elegant satire (classical/Attic irony) rather than harsh, corrosive invective. Small, well-placed ironies often achieve reform better than sustained, mordant abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language for weighty matters
rubrics_metrics.description: “The plainest words are the most profitable oratory in the weightiest matters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling serious subjects in satire or prose, favor simple, direct diction over abstruse or ornate language. Plain speech makes moral and political critique more persuasive and accessible.
